description: A diverse group of developers and AI enthusiasts based on RSR Technica Industries engineering company
summary:
Problem
Long missions, lunar operations and deep-space flights expose astronauts to microgravity, radiation, isolation and communication delays. Fluid shifts raise intracranial pressure and cause SANS, increase thrombosis risk, speed bone and muscle loss and disrupt circadian rhythms. Early symptoms go unnoticed until critical, because rare clinical checks don’t compare continuous telemetry with each person’s own baseline.

Solution
Crew Health is a multi-layer health-monitoring and clinical decision-support platform for lunar habitats and spacecraft, with views for astronauts and the Flight Surgeon. It turns wearable, environmental, check-in and lab data into alerts and countermeasures on three levels: Normal, Attention, Critical.

Key features

TODAY: 3D body map; 24-hour vitals (HR, HRV, SpO2, respiration, skin temp, BP) vs. personal pre-flight baseline
Radiation & habitat: daily, mission and career dose (600 mSv limit), SPE warnings, CO2, pressure, temperature, humidity
SLEEP: sleep stages, sleep debt, bedtime-linked cabin lighting
LABS: blood, urine, saliva, ultrasound and eye exams vs. baseline
CHECK-IN: mood, symptoms, hydration, menstrual tracking, PVT reaction test
ACTIONS: first-aid protocols, daily countermeasures, Flight Surgeon console

All thresholds are based on NASA HRP research and NASA-STD-3001.
details:
All data shown is synthetic. The app supports decisions; it does not diagnose, prescribe treatment or replace the flight surgeon.
  • Presentation — https://canva.link/qug79h97vf9sgwl
  • Backend (API + health engine) — https://gitlab.com/nsac_26_rti_hack/backend
  • Web app (tablet / desktop) — https://gitlab.com/nsac_26_rti_hack/frontend
  • Phone app — https://gitlab.com/nsac_26_rti_hack/mobile

The summary above covers the problem and our solution. Here we show who uses Crew Health, walk through the app in 8 screens, explain how the assessment works and share the research behind it.

1. Who uses it

  • Astronaut (tablet or phone) — Sees: Only their own data — Can do: Daily check-in, reaction-time test, enter test results, follow action cards and the daily plan
  • Flight surgeon (mission doctor) — Sees: Every crew member of their mission — Can do: Review alerts, set personal ranges, order tests, send recommendations and daily plans

2. Walkthrough in 8 screens

All screenshots come from the working app with the synthetic demo crew of mission Halcyon-2 (lunar surface habitat, day 46).

2.1 Today — the astronaut's main screen

  • Astronaut figure in the centre: 8 body systems (head, eyes, heart, lungs, thermal, metabolic, musculoskeletal, reproductive). Each point is coloured by status; labels sit at the height of the body part.
  • Top line: "5 / 7 systems normal" + overall status, so the astronaut knows in one second whether something is wrong.
  • Action required card, today's tasks (check-in, exercise vs. the 120-min plan), vitals for the last 24 h compared with the personal range, sleep, radiation (today / mission / career dose vs. the NASA 600 mSv limit, solar-event alert) and cabin air (CO2, pressure, temperature, humidity vs. NASA-STD-3001).
  • Good to know: short facts with their source.

2.2 Tap a body system → details

The selected system opens on the left: a plain-language explanation ("microgravity shifts body fluids toward the head…"), the trend chart with personal and critical limits, every measurement with its status, and the linked NASA hazard.

2.3 Action card — first aid and next steps

When the engine finds a problem (here: reaction time 57 % slower than the astronaut's own baseline), it opens a card with numbered steps, a re-measure timer, red flags ("call the crew now") and when to call for help. Texts that are not yet verified carry a visible demo — requires verification tag.

2.4 Daily check-in (one minute, glove-friendly buttons)

Mood, stress, fatigue, sleep quality, free text "in your own words", symptoms, vision self-check (SANS), food, fluids, urine colour, body mass, and a cycle section (flow, pain, menstrual suppression and dose) shown only for astronauts who track it. Ends with a 10-tap reaction-time test (PVT-style). Can be edited during the day.

2.5 Medical tests — schedule, results, history

Blood, 24-h urine, saliva, stool, neck-vein and eye ultrasound, eye OCT, cognition battery. The schedule shows what is overdue / due today / planned; each result is compared with the normal range and with the astronaut's pre-flight baseline (%); out-of-range values explain what to do and who decides. History chart per test.

2.6 Personal checklist from the flight surgeon

Training, medication and activity items (e.g. resistance exercise, vitamin D, bright light in the morning, wind-down before sleep) with done / overdue / open state and a 7-day adherence table.

2.7 Flight-surgeon console

Crew sorted by severity, each with a ring of body-system statuses and key numbers; mission KPIs (critical / attention, unacknowledged alerts, active recommendations, highest radiation dose); the alert feed with Acknowledge; a last-7-days worst-status grid per astronaut; habitat air. From here the doctor opens any astronaut, edits personal ranges, orders tests and sends recommendations.

2.8 Same app on a phone

The layout adapts to a phone; a separate native phone app (React Native) uses the same API. All touch targets are at least 48 px so they can be used with gloves.

Also in the app (not pictured): sleep tracker (night timeline, stages vs. typical range, sleep debt, suggested lights-out time and pre-sleep cabin lighting), notifications, crew photos and profile cards, personal-range editor with reason, review date and change history.

3. How the assessment works

  • Personal baseline, not population average. Each value is compared with the astronaut's own pre-flight normal; the flight surgeon can adjust the range (reason required, history kept).
  • Persistence matters. Behavioural and sleep changes count only when they last (e.g. ≥ 3 days), so a single bad day does not trigger an alarm.
  • Connections between signals: headache ↔ cabin CO2, fatigue ↔ short sleep, temperature ↔ cycle phase.
  • Escalation: normal → attention (self-care steps, re-measure) → critical (first-aid card, crew and flight surgeon notified). Alerts open, escalate and close automatically when values return to normal.
  • Rules are data, not code. Every threshold, text, hazard link and source lives in one rules.json; the same file is used by the server and the apps. Values without a verified source are flagged demo / requires_verification and the UI shows it.

4. Architecture (short)

  • Health engine — Technology: Pure Python functions — Why: Data in → statuses out; no database or network, fully unit-tested
  • Rules — Technology: rules.json — Why: Thresholds, texts, zones, hazards and sources in one reviewable file
  • API — Technology: Django + REST framework, JWT, PostgreSQL, Docker — Why: Roles and mission-based access
  • Web app — Technology: Plain HTML / CSS / JS, local Chart.js — Why: No external CDN — works on an isolated network
  • Phone app — Technology: React Native / Expo (TypeScript) — Why: Same API
  • Data — Technology: Synthetic generator — Why: 2 missions, 6 astronauts, 2 doctors; sensors every 5 minutes, 60 days of check-ins and tests

Built for future offline use on board: every record carries a client UUID and timestamp, and batch upload is idempotent (safe to resend after a lost link). About 70 automated tests cover the engine and the API.

5. Research summary

Sources: NASA Human Research Program (hazards, risks, ongoing research, Precision Health), NASA-STD-3001, NASA OCHMO technical briefs, CSA, peer-reviewed spaceflight studies (section 8) and expert interviews (section 6).

5.1 What we monitor and why

  • Radiation — What spaceflight does: ISS crews receive ~150–250 mSv per year, hundreds of times Earth background; solar particle events cause spikes — What the app does: Daily, mission and career dose; % of the career limit; shelter alert on a solar event
  • Vision and head (SANS) — What spaceflight does: Fluids shift toward the head and raise pressure around the brain; many astronauts show eye changes — What the app does: Head / eyes zones, daily vision self-check, eye ultrasound and OCT results
  • Heart and blood flow — What spaceflight does: Circulation changes, arteries stiffen, clot risk rises (jugular vein) — What the app does: Heart rate, HRV, blood pressure vs. personal baseline; hematocrit, D-dimer; neck-vein ultrasound
  • Bones and muscles — What spaceflight does: Fast bone loss and muscle atrophy — What the app does: Exercise vs. daily plan, checklist adherence, urine calcium and bone markers
  • Sleep and mind — What spaceflight does: Isolation, confinement and a shifted day/night cycle disrupt sleep, mood and cognition — What the app does: Sleep tracker, mood / stress / fatigue check-in, reaction-time test, cognition battery, lighting advice
  • Cabin air — What spaceflight does: High CO2 causes headaches and lower performance — What the app does: CO2 1-h and 7-day averages, pressure, temperature, humidity linked to symptoms
  • Biomarkers — What spaceflight does: Blood, urine, saliva and stool show immune status, stress hormones, inflammation, microbiome, bone turnover — What the app does: Periodic tests compared with the pre-flight baseline
  • Women's health — What spaceflight does: Menstrual suppression is common; breakthrough bleeding and missed doses need attention — What the app does: Cycle tracking, alerts on breakthrough bleeding, missed dose, pain ≥ 4, long delay

5.2 Verified NASA limits used by the engine

  • Career radiation dose < 600 mSv (same for all ages and sexes); solar particle event < 250 mSv; long missions: < 1.3 mSv/day in free space, < 0.9 mSv/day on a planetary surface (NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1, OCHMO-TB-020).
  • Cabin CO2: 1-hour average ≤ 3 mmHg, 7-day average < 2.5 mmHg (headache risk < 1 %); cabin pressure 34.5–103 kPa (NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2, OCHMO-TB-004).

5.3 Illustrative alert tiers from our research notes (marked demo, to be verified)

  • Hematocrit: normal 40–50 % (men), 36–44 % (women); attention above ~52–54 %; critical above ~55–58 % (clot risk).
  • Blood pressure: attention if systolic > 140 or < 90 mmHg; critical > 160 or a fainting-level drop.
  • Sleep: attention < 6 h for 3 nights; critical < 4–5 h for a week together with falling cognitive scores.

5.4 How samples are collected in flight

Blood in vacuum tubes, centrifuged and frozen on board; urine in sealed containers with preservative (24-h collection); saliva with sterile swabs; neck-vein and eye ultrasound guided remotely from the ground; actigraphy plus a short computer cognition battery.

6. Expert input

  • Clayton Anderson, former NASA astronaut (167 days in space, six spacewalks): the hardest parts of long-mission health are sleep shifting and the basics — heart rate, blood pressure, VO2 max. This shaped our focus on sleep and personal baselines.
  • Dr. Leila Asylbekova, psychologist developing assessment methods: spaceflight affects cognition and performance, so psychological state is tracked alongside physical health — without stigma and only on sustained change.

7. Limitations and next steps

  • Replace demo thresholds with values verified against NASA HRP sources together with flight surgeons.
  • Connect real wearables and habitat sensors instead of the simulator; full offline mode on board.
  • Optional sharing with family on Earth (the privacy of behavioural data must be decided first).
  • An on-board assistant that gives first advice before the doctor answers (concept).
  • Not a medical device; synthetic data only.
